lead: Logic is the grammar of proof. This unit shows how to translate statements into symbols, test whether an argument is valid, and prove claims by direct, contrapositive, contradiction and induction methods. By the end you can read a truth table, build normal forms, use inference rules and write short correct proofs.
about: This unit teaches how to write and test logical statements, and how to prove them. Chapter 1.1 starts with propositions, connectives and truth tables; 1.2 turns truth tables into laws of logic and the contrapositive. Chapter 1.3 puts formulas into DNF, CNF, PDNF and PCNF, and 1.4 uses those forms in rules of inference for valid arguments. Chapter 1.5 adds consistency tests and the CP rule; 1.6 moves from propositions to predicates and quantifiers. Chapter 1.7 covers direct, indirect and contradiction proofs; 1.8 covers induction and strong induction with Peano axioms; 1.9 gives resolution for propositional and predicate logic. After the unit, a student can test an argument, simplify a formula and choose a proof method.

chapters.idea: A proposition is a statement with a definite truth value, and connectives combine propositions into truth tables that reveal tautologies.
chapters.depth: Cover propositions versus sentences, truth values T and F, negation ¬, conjunction ∧, disjunction ∨, exclusive or ⊕, implication →, biconditional ↔, precedence, truth tables up to three variables, tautology, contradiction and contingency. Some syllabi call exclusive or XOR and call biconditional equivalence. Keep the bitwise AND, OR and XOR demonstration as a short illustration only.

figure.title: (p→q)∨(q→p)
figure.aria: A four-row truth table for (p→q)∨(q→p); the last column is true in every row.

chapters.example: Construct the truth table for (p→q)∨(q→p). Classify the formula as a tautology, contradiction or contingency. Answer: all four rows give T, so it is a tautology.
chapters.trap: Implication p→q is false only when p is true and q is false; do not treat it as q→p.
chapters.leave: Logical equivalence laws to 1.2, normal forms to 1.3, and quantified statements to 1.6.

chapters.idea: Logical equivalences are laws that let you replace one formula by another with the same truth value, and the contrapositive is the equivalent form of an implication.
chapters.depth: Cover laws of logic equivalences and implications: identity, domination, idempotent, double negation, commutative, associative, distributive, De Morgan, absorption and implication. Cover converse, inverse and contrapositive of p→q, and show that only the contrapositive is equivalent to p→q. Some syllabi call the laws of logic identities.

figure.title: Simplifying (p→q)∧(p∨q)
figure.aria: A five-step vertical simplification; the final box q is the simplified formula.

chapters.example: Simplify ((p→q)∧(p∨q)) using laws of logic. Also write the converse and contrapositive of p→q. Answer: the formula simplifies to q; the converse is q→p; the contrapositive is ¬q→¬p.
chapters.trap: The converse and inverse are not equivalent to the original implication; only the contrapositive is.
chapters.leave: Canonical normal forms to 1.3, quantified equivalences to 1.6.

chapters.idea: Normal forms rewrite a formula as a standard sum of products or product of sums, and the principal forms list exactly the truth-table rows that matter.
chapters.depth: Cover literals, minterms, maxterms, DNF, CNF, PDNF and PCNF. PDNF is also called full DNF or principal disjunctive normal form; PCNF is also called full CNF or principal conjunctive normal form. Show how to read them from a truth table and how to convert by laws of logic. Keep the treatment propositional.

figure.title: f(p,q)=p⊕q
figure.aria: A four-row truth table for XOR; the two true output rows give the minterms for PDNF.

chapters.example: Find the PDNF and PCNF of f(p,q)=p⊕q. Answer: PDNF is (¬p∧q)∨(p∧¬q); PCNF is (p∨q)∧(¬p∨¬q).
chapters.trap: For a minterm a variable is unnegated when it is 1; for a maxterm it is negated when it is 1. DNF is not automatically PDNF.
chapters.leave: Resolution uses CNF in 1.9; Boolean algebra uses normal forms in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A valid argument follows from its premises by named rules of inference, not by intuition.
chapters.depth: Cover argument, premises, conclusion, validity, and the standard rules: modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism, addition, simplification, conjunction, and constructive and destructive dilemma. Show a formal proof as a numbered sequence. Mention the resolution rule only as a bridge to 1.9.

figure.title: Proof of r
figure.aria: A proof diagram: p and p→q give q; q and q→r give r.

chapters.example: Premises: p→q, q→r, p. Prove r. Give a step-by-step valid argument. Answer: p and p→q give q by modus ponens; q and q→r give r by modus ponens.
chapters.trap: Affirming the consequent (q, p→q therefore p) and denying the antecedent (¬p, p→q therefore ¬q) are invalid.
chapters.leave: Consistency and CP rule to 1.5; quantified rules to 1.6; resolution to 1.9.

chapters.idea: A set of premises is consistent when all can be true together, and the CP rule proves an implication by temporarily assuming its antecedent.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover consistency and inconsistency of propositional premises, testing by truth table or derivation, the CP rule also called conditional proof, and the indirect proof or inconsistency method. Keep the treatment short and focus on clear discharge of the temporary assumption.

figure.title: CP proof of p→r
figure.aria: A conditional-proof flow: assume p, derive q and r, then discharge p to conclude p→r.

chapters.example: Using the CP rule, prove p→r from the premises p→q and q→r. Then state whether p→q, q→r, p, ¬r are consistent. Answer: assume p, get q by MP, get r by MP, so p→r; the four premises are inconsistent because p gives r and ¬r clashes.
chapters.trap: The CP assumption is temporary: discharge it before the final line, and do not list it as a premise of the theorem.
chapters.leave: Full resolution refutation to 1.9; proof methods in 1.7.

chapters.idea: Predicate logic adds variables and quantifiers so a statement can speak about all or some objects in a chosen universe.
chapters.depth: Cover predicate, variable, universe of discourse also called domain, universal ∀, existential ∃, uniqueness ∃!, free and bound variables, negation of quantifiers, logical equivalences and implications for quantified statements, rules of specification such as universal instantiation, and rules of generalization such as universal generalization and existential generalization. Include validity of quantified arguments.

figure.aria: Three nested sets: the BTech set with Ravi sits inside the discrete-math set, which sits inside the universe.

chapters.example: All BTech students study discrete mathematics. Ravi is a BTech student. Using predicates and quantifiers, prove that Ravi studies discrete mathematics. Answer: write ∀x(B(x)→D(x)) and B(Ravi); universal specification gives B(Ravi)→D(Ravi); modus ponens gives D(Ravi).
chapters.trap: Changing the universe changes truth value; ¬∀xP(x) is ∃x¬P(x), not ∀x¬P(x).
chapters.leave: Quantified proof templates to 1.7; predicate resolution to 1.9; sets and relations to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A proof method is a chosen route from what is given to what must be shown, and the right route often makes a hard claim easy.
chapters.depth: Cover direct proof, indirect proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, existence proofs and counterexamples. Use definitions of even and odd integers, rational numbers and basic inequalities. Some syllabi call indirect proof the contrapositive method. Show how to write a proof in clear steps.

figure.title: Direct proof: n odd → n² odd
figure.aria: A direct proof chain: assume n=2k+1, square it, regroup as twice an integer plus one, conclude n² is odd.

chapters.example: Prove directly: if n is an odd integer, then n² is odd. Answer: let n=2k+1 with k an integer; then n²=4k²+4k+1=2(2k²+2k)+1, which has the odd form 2m+1.
chapters.trap: In proof by contradiction of P→Q, assume P∧¬Q, not just ¬Q alone.
chapters.leave: Induction to 1.8; number-theory proofs to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Mathematical induction proves an infinite family of statements by a base case and a step that carries truth from one case to the next.
chapters.depth: Cover the principle of mathematical induction, base step, inductive step, strong induction, well-ordering and the Peano axioms for natural numbers. Some syllabi start at n=1, others at n=0; state the starting value. Use sums, inequalities and divisibility examples. Keep Peano axioms brief and clear.

figure.title: Induction for 1+3+...+(2n−1)=n²
figure.aria: An induction flow: prove P(1), assume P(k), add the next odd term, factor to (k+1)², and conclude P(k+1).

chapters.example: Prove by induction that 1+3+5+...+(2n−1)=n² for every integer n≥1. Answer: for n=1, 1=1²; assume the sum up to 2k−1 is k²; add 2k+1 to get k²+2k+1=(k+1)², so P(k+1) holds.
chapters.trap: Both base case and inductive step are needed; in weak induction you may assume only P(k), not all earlier cases.
chapters.leave: Recurrence solving to Unit 3; Peano-based algebra details beyond the statement of axioms to later courses.

chapters.idea: Resolution proves a claim by adding its negation as clauses and deriving the empty clause.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover clauses, CNF, the resolution rule, refutation, the empty clause, and the extension to predicate logic with substitution, unification and Skolemization in outline. Keep proofs short and show the clause form clearly.

figure.aria: A resolution tree ending in the empty clause: q is derived from p∨q and ¬p, then clashes with ¬q.

chapters.example: Use resolution to prove q from the premises p∨q and ¬p. Answer: clauses are {p,q} and {¬p}; add the negated goal {¬q}; resolve {p,q} with {¬p} to get {q}; resolve {q} with {¬q} to get the empty clause □.
chapters.trap: Resolution proves by refutation: negate the conclusion, convert to clauses, and derive the empty clause; do not resolve an implication directly.
chapters.leave: Full unification algorithms and completeness proofs to advanced courses; Boolean algebra to Unit 5.
